column27: Potentially fatal. Mutagen, teratogen. Protein lectin found in castor beans (Ricinus communis), one of the most potent/lethal substances known — ~500μg can kill an adult within days. Castor plant/beans are important commercial industrial crops (castor oil production); waste mash from castor-oil processing is 3-5% ricin by weight. Castor plant is an attractive ornamental found in yards/gardens; found in 25+ US states and other regions (dies in freezing weather). Ricin poisoning can occur via accidental castor-bean ingestion (including bead-necklace use in some countries). Ricin enters cells and inhibits protein synthesis, causing systemic shutdown within hours once this mechanism is halted. Not contagious, doesn't spread person-to-person. Because it's a chemical made by living things rather than a living organism itself, considered less effective as a mass military weapon than pathogens like anthrax/ebola, but poses an accessible terrorist-weapon risk given ease of production/use. Extremely hazardous when freeze-dried (easily dispersed powder) — lab personnel typically directed to avoid freeze-drying it. No known antidote/vaccine/effective therapy exists; antibody-therapy research is ongoing.

column53: Symptoms depend on ricin purity, exposure level/route, and dose. Initial symptoms usually appear 6-10h to 3 days post-exposure (as early as 45min if ingested on an empty stomach). Death can occur 36-72h post-exposure depending on route/dose; victims may linger 10-12 days before death or recovery. Surviving >5 days without complications reduces death likelihood. Inhalation: within hours, respiratory distress, labored breathing, SOB, chest tightness, hypoxemia, fever, cough, nausea, sweating, aching muscles; heavy sweating may precede noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (occurring later, 1-3 days post-exposure, unlike phosgene's ~6h), worsening breathing and causing blue skin; may progress to low blood pressure, blue skin, multisystem organ failure, respiratory failure, death. Skin: uncertain absorption through intact skin (believed low-risk); may be absorbed through damaged/irritated skin or via solvent carrier; sufficient absorption produces ingestion-like symptoms; injection causes local muscle/lymph-node death, potentially leading to liver/kidney failure and death. Eyes: tearing, eyelid swelling, pain, redness, corneal injury. Ingestion: within hours — nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain/cramping, diarrhea (possibly bloody), lowered blood pressure, hallucinations, bloody urine, GI bleeding, low/no urinary output, pupil dilation, fever, thirst, sore throat, headache, vascular collapse, shock; severe vomiting/diarrhea may cause severe dehydration and multisystem organ failure; organs (liver, spleen, kidneys) may fail within days. Late-phase: cytotoxic liver/CNS/kidney/adrenal effects typically 2-5 days post-exposure; patient may be asymptomatic during the preceding 1-5 days (CDC).
column54: Repeated exposure may cause allergic/asthma-like symptoms — nasal/throat congestion, itchy watery eyes, hives, chest tightness, wheezing in acute cases. May affect kidneys, liver, pancreas. Animal studies suggest possible severe human lung damage.

column57: Symptoms resemble other illnesses, especially flu, complicating diagnosis. Lab testing may show metabolic acidosis, elevated liver/renal function tests, hematuria, leukocytosis (2-5× normal).
column58: No antidote exists. Send all exposed persons to nearest hospital emergency department. Have potentially exposed persons shower and change clothes immediately. See a doctor same-day given rapid symptom onset (as little as 1.5 days). Remove ricin from the body as quickly as possible; treatment requires hospital setting; alert medical staff to exposure potential for their own protection and appropriate treatment. If awaiting medical assistance, keep victim comfortable. If ingested: secure airway; gastric lavage may be considered only if performed shortly after ingestion (generally within 1h), weighing GI-tract injury-aggravation risk. Treatment is primarily supportive, tailored to exposure route (inhalation/ingestion/eye/skin). Do NOT induce vomiting. Rinse mouth; flush stomach with activated charcoal if very recently ingested (note: superactivated charcoal may have little value for large molecules like ricin, per USAMRICD); wash eyes with water if red/irritated. Supportive care: IV fluids, circulatory/respiratory support, medications for seizure/low blood pressure; fluid input critical (losses up to 2-2.5L probable). If drowsy/unconscious, give nothing by mouth; if vomiting, lean patient forward or place on left side (head-down if possible) to maintain airway and prevent aspiration. Monitor/restore fluid and electrolyte balance; early aggressive IV fluid/electrolyte replacement. Administer oxygen if breathing is difficult/labored due to pulmonary fluid.
column59: Level A (fully encapsulated suit with SCBA) when entering areas with unknown contaminant/concentration, until monitoring confirms. Recommended materials: Tychem BR or Responder CSM. Decontamination: responders wear Level A when decontaminating a known attack area; otherwise stay away. Move quickly — decontamination delay matters. Only decontaminate aerosolized-ricin scenes with proper equipment/training; do not enter hot zone without them. Even if uncertain of contamination, shower thoroughly and change clothes ASAP post-incident; bag clothing in labeled durable 6-mil polyethylene bags. Decontaminate non-ambulatory victims without touching/entering hot zone if possible; ensure victims are decontaminated before leaving the area to prevent spread; avoid breaking skin, cover open wounds during decon. CDC-recommended decon solution: detergent-water (pH 8-10.5); soft brushes for PPE contamination removal. Household bleach also recommended for people/surface cleanup: fresh daily 0.5% sodium hypochlorite solution (10% household bleach diluted 1:9 with water), 15min contact time; avoid eyes/open wounds (especially abdomen/spine/brain)/mouth; wash off after 15min. Absent pH-adjusted solutions, wash with warm soapy water, using a hose/spray/fog system to avoid touching the victim; begin washing immediately without waiting for soap or clothing removal (down to undergarments). Wash-strip-wash-evacuate protocol: wash first, victim self-removes clothing, wash again (with soap if available), then move upwind/uphill away from hot zone.

column26: One of the most toxic known chemical warfare nerve agents. Exposure can cause death within minutes; 1/10mL on skin can be fatal. column58: Antidote administration is critical but may be difficult in the immediate hazard zone if antidotes/procedures aren't available there. Do NOT administer antidotes preventatively. Diazepam (or other benzodiazepines) given for evidence of seizures (moderate-severe exposure). Inhalation: hold breath until protective mask donned; for severe signs (chest tightness, pupil constriction, coordination loss), administer all three Nerve Agent Antidote Kit Mark I injectors in rapid succession (or atropine per physician direction); may repeat at 5-20min intervals up to three injection series, no further without medical direction, with injection record maintained; artificial respiration if breathing stopped (mouth-to-mouth only if approved delivery systems unavailable and no facial contamination); administer oxygen if breathing difficult; seek medical attention immediately. Eyes: flush immediately with water 10-15min, then don protective mask; miosis alone (without other signs) doesn't warrant injection — take individual to medical facility for observation instead. Skin: don protective mask, remove contaminated clothing, immediately wash with copious soap/water, 10% sodium carbonate solution, or 5% liquid household bleach, rinse well; administer Mark I Kit intramuscular injection only if local sweating/muscular twitching observed; seek medical attention immediately. Ingestion: do NOT induce vomiting (first symptoms likely GI); immediately administer Mark I kit autoinjector intramuscular injection. Medical treatment: monitor ECG and respiration/ventilation adequacy; supplemental oxygenation, frequent secretion suctioning, endotracheal intubation, assisted ventilation may be required; diazepam (5-10mg adults, 0.2-0.5mg/kg children) for convulsion control (lorazepam/other benzodiazepines usable; barbiturates/phenytoin/other anticonvulsants ineffective); atropine administration (if not already given) should precede benzodiazepines for optimal seizure control; inhalation-exposed patients with chest pain/tightness/cough should be observed/examined periodically for 6-12h to detect delayed bronchitis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or respiratory failure (NIOSH).
column59: Level A PPE: rubber gloves, protective clothing, goggles, respirators, butyl rubber gloves (M3/M4, Norton chemical protective glove set), Tyvek 'F' decontamination suit for barrier protection against chemical warfare agents. Airtight impermeable clothing (butyl rubber or coated fabric) for personnel entering heavily contaminated areas; may be penetrated after hours of heavy-concentration exposure — liquid contamination must be neutralized/removed ASAP. Published swatch-test breakthrough times (various commercial Level A suits/gloves) generally exceed 225-480min for GB. Call US Soldier and Biological Chemical Command/Edgewood Research Development and Engineering Center if proper equipment/training unavailable. Contact lenses not permitted; splash-proof goggles+face shield unless full-face respiratory protection worn; wash immediately if skin wet/contaminated; emergency showers/eyewash provided.

column68: Cover spills with vermiculite/diatomaceous earth/clay/fine sand/sponges/paper-cloth towels. Decontaminate with copious ≥10wt% aqueous NaOH solution. column69: Highly volatile poison (organophosphate); vapor/skin/eye contact or swallowing can kill, symptoms may be delayed hours. If exposure occurs, remove/isolate gear immediately, thoroughly decontaminate personnel. Storage containers may explode/rocket. Vapors heavier than air, collect in low areas. Combustion products (CO, fluorine, phosphorus oxide) less deadly than the material itself. Reacts with steam/water producing toxic corrosive vapors. Evacuate all non-firefighting personnel; contain fires to prevent uncontrolled-area contamination. Positive-pressure full face-piece NIOSH-approved SCBA required where oxygen deficiency risk exists or per fire chief/CAI officer direction; appropriate protective-clothing levels for rescue/reconnaissance responders. Complete protection required; have decontaminants (bleach, alkali) and atropine available. Dry chemical/CO2/foam extinguishers. Cool exposed containers from secure location with water spray; withdraw if venting sound rises or tank discolors.
column70: Open-pit burning or burying of GB or GB-contaminated items in any quantity is prohibited. Detoxified GB (per decontamination procedures) can be thermally destroyed by incineration in an EPA-approved incinerator per RCRA regulations. Decontamination chemistry: minimum 56g decon solution per gram GB; agitate ≥1h; final pH must exceed 11.5 (add NaOH as needed to sustain pH>11.5 for 60min) using 10% NaOH, or alternatively 10wt% sodium carbonate (agitate 1h, react 3h total, final pH>10), or 5.25% sodium hypochlorite, or 25wt% monoethylamine (MEA, fully dissolved in water before agent addition) at the same 56g:1g ratio with 1h agitation. Scoop material into fully removable-head HDPE-lined drum; cover with decon solution before sealing; decontaminate/label drum exterior per IAW/EPA/DOT regs; overpack leaking containers with vermiculite; dispose of exterior-decontamination material per IAW/federal/state/local regs; conduct general-area monitoring to confirm atmospheric concentrations remain below exposure limits.

column58: Antidote administration is critical. Skin: don protective mask, remove contaminated clothing, immediately wash with copious soap/water, 10% sodium carbonate solution, or 5% liquid household bleach, rinse well; administer Mark I Kit intramuscular injection only if local sweating/muscular twitching observed; seek medical attention immediately. column58: No antidote exists for nitrogen mustard toxicity. Because health effects may not occur until several hours after exposure, patients/victims should be observed in a hospital setting for at least 24h. Gastric lavage is contraindicated following ingestion due to esophagus/upper-airway perforation risk. Eyes: irrigate ≥15 min, seek care. Skin: remove clothing, wash immediately with soap/water, speed is of extreme importance, seek care. Inhaled: remove, rescue breathing/CPR. Swallowed: large water + induce vomiting (not if unconscious). Keep victim quiet, maintain normal body temperature; effects may be delayed, keep victim under observation. Decontamination: of all potentially exposed areas within minutes after exposure is the only effective means of decreasing tissue damage (per NIOSH). Remove clothes and place contaminated clothes/personal belongings in a sealed double bag. Decontamination should be performed within the first 2min following exposure to prevent tissue damage; if not accomplished in the first several minutes, decontamination should still be performed to remove residual liquid mustard or trapped mustard vapor from skin/clothes, preventing vapor off-gassing or cross-contamination of responders/facilities. Physical removal of the agent — not detoxification/neutralization — is the most important decontamination principle; mustard is not detoxified by water alone and remains in decontamination effluent (dilute) absent hydrolysis. Vapor-exposed patients: remove all clothing in clean air, shampoo/rinse hair to prevent vapor off-gassing. Liquid-exposed patients: wash in warm/hot water at least 3 times using liquid soap (dispose/replace container after use), large water volumes, mild-to-moderate friction with a single-use sponge/washcloth for the first two washes (avoid brush scrubbing — may enhance absorption via skin damage); third wash rinses with large warm/hot water amounts; shampoo for hair; if warm/hot water unavailable but cold water is, use cold water rather than delaying decontamination; rinse eyes/mucous membranes/open wounds with sterile saline or water. Health-care providers should verify adequate decontamination (repeating the process if inadequate) before facility entry, be prepared to stabilize conventional injuries during decontamination, and wear proper PPE.

column58: Immediate decontamination of even the smallest drop is essential; use M291 Skin Decontamination Kit. Inhalation: hold breath until respiratory protective mask donned; if severe exposure signs appear (chest tightness, pupil constriction, coordination loss), immediately administer all three Nerve Agent Antidote Kit Mark 1 injectors in rapid succession (or atropine per local physician direction); may repeat at 5-20min intervals if symptoms progress, up to three series; no further injections without medical direction; maintain injection record; give artificial respiration if breathing stopped (avoid mouth-to-mouth with facial contamination); administer oxygen if breathing difficult; seek care immediately. Eyes: flush with water 10-15min, then don respiratory protective mask; miosis alone does not warrant injection — take to medical facility for observation instead. Skin: don respirator/protective mask, remove contaminated clothing, immediately wash with 5% household bleach solution, rinse well with water then soap and water; administer Mark I antidote kit only if local sweating/muscular twitching present; seek care immediately. Ingestion: do not induce vomiting (first symptoms likely GI); immediately administer Mark I antidote kit; seek care immediately. Medical observation recommended. Medical treatment: ECG and respiration/ventilation adequacy monitored; supplemental oxygenation, frequent secretion suctioning, endotracheal intubation, assisted ventilation may be required; diazepam (5-10mg adults, 0.2-0.5mg/kg children) may control convulsions; lorazepam/other benzodiazepines may be used (barbiturates, phenytoin, other anticonvulsants ineffective); atropine (if not already given) should precede benzodiazepines for best seizure control; inhalation-exposed patients with chest pain/tightness/cough should be observed 6-12h for delayed bronchitis, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or respiratory failure. Decontamination water is itself dangerous — ensure victims are adequately decontaminated before release to avoid spreading agent. Rinse eyes/mucous membranes/open wounds with sterile saline or water, then move upwind/uphill away from hot zone. Additional decontaminants beyond household bleach: bleach solids/powders/solutions (NaOCl or Ca(OCl)2); DS2 (2% NaOH, 70% diethylenetriamine, 28% ethylene glycol monomethyl ether); NaOH-moistened towelettes with phenol/ethanol/ammonia. column70: This entry describes standard published field/laboratory detoxification and destruction procedures, not synthesis or weaponization information. Field procedures (quantities >50g, requiring qualified-expert/safety-officer approval): prepare alcoholic calcium hypochlorite (HTH) mixture (100mL denatured ethanol + 900mL 10% HTH slurry in water, made just before use); use 14g of this mixture per gram of VX, agitating during VX addition and for ≥1h minimum (reaction is exothermic with substantial off-gassing — route evolved gases through a decontaminant-filled scrubber before filtered release); after agitation, add 10% sodium hydroxide to maintain pH 12.5 for ≥24h, then hold pH 10-12 for ≥90 days to prevent hazardous intermediate formation; decontaminate/label drum exterior per EPA/DOT regulations; overpack leaking containers with vermiculite between interior/exterior containers; conduct area air monitoring to confirm compliance with airborne exposure limits. If HTH mixture unavailable, alternative decontaminants in order of preference: DS2 (2% NaOH, 70% diethylenetriamine, 28% ethylene glycol monomethyl ether), Supertropical Bleach Slurry (STB), sodium hypochlorite. Open-pit burning or burying of VX or VX-contaminated items in any quantity is prohibited. Detoxified VX may be thermally destroyed by incineration in an EPA-approved incinerator per RCRA provisions. Several states classify decontaminated surety material as RCRA Hazardous Waste. Laboratory procedures (quantities <50g): if HTH active chlorine ≥55%, use 80g of 10% slurry per gram VX (proportionally more if chlorine activity <55%); agitate during addition and for ≥1h minimum; if phasing continues past 5min, add denatured ethanol (10wt% of total agent/decon) to assist miscibility (minimize ethanol to avoid hazardous-waste formation); after 1h agitation, adjust mixture to pH 10-11; conduct area air monitoring to confirm compliance.

column26: Grayish-white, lustrous metal as platelets, flakes, or bluish-black amorphous powder. Powdered metal is a fire/explosion hazard — may ignite spontaneously, can continue burning under water. Never found free in nature; most common sources are ores zircon and baddeleyite. Generally produced by chloride or iodide reduction; the metal is very reactive, production carried out under inert-gas atmosphere.
column27: 'Getter' in vacuum tubes; metallurgy deoxidizer; platinum substitute; explosive-mixture priming; flashlight powders; lamp filaments; flash bulbs; rayon-spinneret construction. Zirconium/alloys (nickel, cobalt, niobium, tantalum) used as pump/pipe lining materials for chemical processes and reaction vessels. Pure zirconium: atomic-reactor structural material; alloyed (particularly with aluminum), a cladding material for water-moderated nuclear reactor fuel rods. Zirconium-columbium alloy: excellent superconductor. Zircon (ZrSiO4): foundry sand, abrasive, refractory (with zirconia), casting-mold coating, alkyl/alkenyl hydrocarbon manufacture catalyst, silicone-rubber stabilizer, gemstone; ceramics glaze/enamel opacifier, fritted glass filters. Zircon and zirconia (zirconium oxide, ZrO2) bricks: glass-furnace linings. Zirconia: metal die extrusion, metal-pouring spout linings, oxyhydrogen-flame lime substitute, pigment, abrasive, incandescent lights, enamel/white-glass/refractory-crucible manufacture. Other zirconium compounds: metal cutting tools, thermocouple jackets, textile waterproofing, ceramics, dermatitis/poison-ivy treatment.
column28: Violent reactions with oxidizers, air, alkali hydroxides, alkali metal compounds (chromates, dichromates, molybdates, salts, sulfates, tungstates), borax, carbon tetrachloride, lead, lead oxide, phosphorus, potassium compounds. Incompatible with boron, carbon, nitrogen, halogens, lead, platinum, potassium nitrate. Powder may ignite spontaneously, continue burning under water. Explodes if mixed with hydrated borax when heated. Fine powder may be stored completely immersed in water.
